extracted.intended_audience: aspiring improvisers, improv teachers, and performers learning long-form improv (The Harold)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing and teaching The Harold — a long-form improvisation format that emphasizes pattern recognition, subversion, ensemble play, scene variety, and economical use of material. The page is a textbook/product description aimed at learners and practitioners of improvisational theatre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern recognition and subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizes pattern recognition and subversion of the audience’s expectations, which are important factors for making people laugh without ever telling a joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recognizable patterns (themes, repeated beats) and then subvert them to create humor; rely on pattern-based payoffs rather than set jokes. Avoid purely joke-based or one-liner approaches that do not build or manipulate patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make people laugh without telling a joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Making people laugh through improvisational structure and choices rather than by delivering prepared jokes or punchlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on scene-work, patterns, callbacks, and subversion to generate laughter organically; anti-patterns include defaulting to rehearsed jokes or forcing punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensemble size and collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Harold involves six to seven players.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design scenes, beats, and group dynamics to accommodate a mid-sized ensemble; coordinate transfers of focus and ensure all players are contributing to pattern development and callbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene and format variety
rubrics_metrics.description: The Harold includes many kinds of scenes: games, monologues, songs, skits and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a mix of formats (games, monologues, songs, skits) within a performance to create textural variety and multiple opportunities for pattern emergence and payoff. Avoid monotonous use of a single scene type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-linear structure
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct shows that do not follow a single linear plot but instead interweave scenes and callbacks; rely on thematic or pattern connections rather than chronological causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory and economy: 'remembers everything and wastes nothing'
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful improvising within the Harold 'remembers everything and wastes nothing' — earlier material is recalled and reused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep careful mental (and performed) track of earlier beats, lines, and details to enable callbacks and repurposing; avoid abandoning useful material. Treat prior offers as resources to be honored and woven into later scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unpredictability and keep audiences guessing
rubrics_metrics.description: The Harold is 'bound to keep both actors and audience members guessing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surprise, reversals, and unexpected connections to sustain engagement; balance surprise with the trust that callbacks and pattern payoffs will satisfy the audience. Avoid predictable or overly safe choices that remove suspense.
